sections.html:
Whitehall sits in Lehigh County, just north of Allentown, and runs under a home rule charter. For a seller, the office that counts is the township building on MacArthur Road, where a mandatory resale inspection sets the pace of any closing.

About 29,405 people live here, in 11,664 households. Owners occupy roughly 62 percent of homes, the midpoint home value is $262,100, and household income at the midpoint is $75,658. Buyers often compare the township with other Lehigh Valley suburbs, and the Whitehall-Coplay School District is a main draw for families.

sections.h2: Resale inspection and certificate of occupancy
sections.html:
Resale triggers a township inspection. Any change of use or occupancy, a home sale among them, also calls for a certificate of occupancy. Each time a property is offered for sale or lease it needs a fresh inspection and a new certificate, even when a rental turns over several times in a year.

The Certificate of Occupancy Application and Guide sets out the steps:

  • Send the inspection request form and the fee to the Bureau of Development, 3219 MacArthur Road.
  • An inspector contacts you within 1 to 3 business days, and the visit is set within 5 to 10 business days.
  • If nothing is wrong, the clear certificate is issued within 1 to 3 business days.
  • Pay by cash, check or money order. Cards are not accepted.

Stack those windows and the paperwork alone runs two to three weeks. Ask for the inspection the day you pick a settlement date.

sections.h2: Inspection fees and what inspectors check
sections.html:
Whitehall Township inspection and permit charges
ServiceCharge
Single-family resale inspection$65
Apartment unit inspection$35 per unit
Conditional certificate for an as-is single-family sale$65 plus a $100 deposit
Conditional certificate for a rental of up to five units$100 plus a $250 deposit
Moving permit$5

Call the township at 610-437-5524 to confirm amounts before you mail a check.

The visit is a targeted safety inspection, narrower than a full home inspection. The checklist includes working smoke detectors on every level and in each sleeping area, a carbon monoxide alarm near bedrooms where a fireplace, attached garage or fuel-burning heater exists, GFCI outlets in kitchens, baths and laundry areas, handrails on stairs of four or more risers, a 100-amp minimum electrical service, a concrete basement floor and visible house numbers at least four inches tall. A missing item is what most often sinks a first inspection.

You have two paths. Fix the violations and have the inspector return, or sell as-is with a conditional certificate. Repairs must be corrected and reinspected within 30 days or before settlement.

For an as-is sale, the seller gives the inspection report to the other party, and a notarized Buyer or Seller Acceptance Form goes back to the township along with the added fees. The conditional certificate allows the transfer only. Nobody can move in until all required repairs pass inspection, and the deposit comes back once a clear certificate is issued in the allotted time.

Heirs, landlords and owners who put off repairs often cannot clear a punch list before closing, and the conditional route suits them. Whoever the buyer is, ask who signs the acceptance form and who does the repairs.

sections.h2: Transfer tax and recording in Lehigh County
sections.html:
The state's realty transfer tax is 1 percent of value, and grantor and grantee are jointly and severally liable for it. County recorders typically take it together with any local transfer tax. No payment, no recording. The municipal and school district share is set locally, so get the rate for a Whitehall address from the Recorder or your closing agent.

  • The Lehigh County Recorder of Deeds is at the courthouse, 455 W. Hamilton Street, Room 122, in Allentown. It is open weekdays, 8:00 AM until 4:30 PM, at 610-782-3162.
  • Deeds between spouses, parent and child, grandparent and grandchild, or siblings usually qualify for an exemption, provided the deed says so.
  • A Statement of Value (REV-183) goes with any transfer that pays less than the full tax, leaves out the full consideration or claims an exemption.

Landlords face one extra rule. Every non-owner-occupied property must name a local responsible agent whose office or home is within 10 miles of the township boundary. That person must be reachable in an emergency and authorized to accept legal service for the owner.

The inspection request form asks whether the property will be a rental and, if so, for the agent's name, address, and daytime and after-hours phone numbers. A tenant who moves out before closing triggers paperwork too, because a moving permit is needed when anyone moves into, out of or within the township. It costs $5 and is issued at the Township Tax Office from 8:00am to 4:00pm.

An owner with a tenant in place can still sell, but the inspector needs access to every room, the attic and the exterior. Give the tenant notice early.

Bring the inspection request form, a check, cash or money order for the fee, and the parcel details to the Bureau of Development. If the house is a rental, add the responsible agent's name, address and phone numbers. For an estate, keep the papers showing who may sign the deed, since the Recorder will not accept a deed from someone without authority.

For the closing itself, your title agent or attorney normally prepares the deed and the Statement of Value, if one is needed. Ask them early which transfer tax rate applies to your address so your net figure is right before you compare offers.

If the house has a tenant, also gather the lease and tell the tenant when the inspector will arrive. Reaching every room, the attic and the exterior on the first visit keeps the process to one trip instead of two.

Work backward from the settlement date. Request the inspection first, since it can take two to three weeks end to end. If it fails, decide quickly between repairing and the conditional certificate, because repairs must pass reinspection within 30 days or before settlement. Collect the deed, payoff figures and any estate papers while you wait.

A cash buyer who accepts the house as-is can shorten the repair stage, but the inspection and certificate still apply. Confirm who will pay the fees and sign the acceptance form before you agree to a closing date.

faqs.q: Can I sell my Whitehall house without a certificate of occupancy?
faqs.a: No. The township requires an inspection and a certificate of occupancy for a resale, and the new owner cannot occupy the property until one is issued. A conditional certificate is available for as-is sales.

faqs.q: How much is the Whitehall resale inspection?
faqs.a: The charge is $65 for a single-family home and $35 per apartment unit. An as-is sale adds a $100 deposit for a house, so call 610-437-5524 to confirm current amounts.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Whitehall house as is if it fails inspection?
faqs.a: Yes. The seller or buyer signs a notarized acceptance form, pays the added fees and receives a conditional certificate that allows the sale only. All listed repairs must pass inspection before anyone occupies the home.

faqs.q: Who pays the transfer tax on a Whitehall home sale?
faqs.a: Buyer and seller are both liable for the 1 percent state tax, and the contract decides how the cost is split. The deed is not recorded until the tax is paid, so your closing agent usually collects it at settlement.

faqs.q: Do I need a local agent if my Whitehall house is a rental?
faqs.a: Yes. A non-owner-occupied property must have a responsible agent within 10 miles of the township. The inspection request form asks for that person's contact details whenever the property is a rental.
